prayer.text: Saint Paul Miki and Companions, pray for us.

cues.text: The Rise and Fall of Christian Japan

Introduced by St. Francis Xavier in 1549, Christianity had spread with remarkable speed through parts of Japan, aided by sympathetic local lords and skillful Jesuit missionaries; by the 1590s several hundred thousand Japanese had been baptized.
This growth increasingly alarmed the powerful regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi , who came to see the foreign religion, and its foreign priests, as a potential vehicle for European political influence.
In 1587 Hideyoshi issued an edict expelling missionaries, though it was inconsistently enforced for a decade.

A diplomatic incident involving a wrecked Spanish galleon in 1596, whose pilot reportedly boasted that missionaries paved the way for eventual conquest, hardened Hideyoshi's suspicion and triggered a sudden, deliberate crackdown.
Arrest and the March to Nagasaki
In early 1597, Hideyoshi ordered the arrest of twenty-six Christians in Kyoto and Osaka.
They included priests, brothers, and laymen: Franciscan friars, Jesuits, members of the Secular Franciscan Order, catechists, doctors, artisans, and several boys as young as twelve.
Among them was Paul Miki , a Japanese-born Jesuit brother from a prominent family, renowned as a gifted preacher only months from ordination to the priesthood.
As a public warning, the prisoners had part of an ear severed and were paraded through towns and villages for public mockery.
They endured a brutal, month-long, six-hundred-mile march from Kyoto to Nagasaki , the center of Japanese Christianity, all the while reportedly singing the Te Deum .
Crucified on Nishizaka Hill
On February 5, 1597 , the twenty-six were bound to crosses arranged in a row on a hill overlooking Nagasaki and killed by spear thrusts through the chest.
From his cross, Paul Miki preached a final sermon to the assembled crowd, declaring himself "a true Japanese."
He was dying not for any foreign cause, but for the Christian doctrine he had freely embraced and taught.
He forgave his executioners in imitation of Christ.

Witnesses reported that the martyrs, ranging from adult priests to boys barely in their teens, met death with visible calm and even joy, an equanimity that astonished many of the officials sent to carry out the execution.
A Church Driven Underground
The execution of the twenty-six martyrs marked the opening of a far longer and more severe persecution of Christianity in Japan.
Over the following decades, missionaries would be expelled entirely, and practicing the faith would become a capital offense.
Remarkably, foreign missionaries finally returned to Japan in the 1860s, after more than two centuries of near-total isolation.

They discovered thriving underground Christian communities around Nagasaki: the Kakure Kirishitan ("hidden Christians"), who had secretly preserved the faith, the sacrament of baptism, and fragments of the liturgy across some seven unbroken generations without any priest at all.

This extraordinary survival is widely regarded as one of the most remarkable instances of lay-sustained faith in Christian history, and is traced directly back to the witness of Paul Miki and his companions.
Legacy
The twenty-six martyrs were beatified in 1627 and canonized together in 1862 by Pope Pius IX, the first martyrs of East Asia to be so honored.
Their feast, kept on February 6 , commemorates the whole group under the collective title of St. Paul Miki and Companions.
The Nishizaka hill execution site in Nagasaki is now marked by a shrine and monument recognized by the Japanese government.
The martyrs’ story remains a touchstone for modern Japan’s small but resilient Catholic community.
Three and a half centuries later, the country would become forever associated in world memory with the atomic destruction of the very city where they died for their faith.
